description: Somos Sakbé, que en maya significa “camino blanco”: el camino hacia las estrellas. Somos 5 ingenieros en Sistemas Automotrices y 1 en Sistemas Computacionales del Instituto Tecnológico Superior del Sur de Guanajuato. Nos apasionan la electrónica, los sensores, la dinámica de vehículos y el software. Construiremos un simulador de misión para astronautas junior con un panel de cabina físico hecho con Arduino. Valoramos la creatividad, el diseño visual y las ganas de aprender.
summary:
Space Survivor es un juego educativo para dos jugadores en el que niños de 7 a 12 años dirigen una base en Marte, con un nivel adicional para secundaria.

El alumno usa un control físico que construimos: un ESP32 con pantalla que muestra el mapa de la base, un joystick para mover al astronauta, botones para elegir agua, energía o escudo, y una perilla para decidir cuánto entregar a cada zona. La computadora muestra la base animada. El docente actúa como la Torre de Control: lanza anomalías basadas en eventos solares reales del Space Weather Database (DONKI) de la NASA y decide cuándo llegan. El aviso viaja a Marte con retraso, como una señal real.

Respondemos al reto convirtiendo las decisiones de una misión en mecánicas de juego: ninguna decisión es gratis, y proteger una zona deja otra expuesta. Cada evento se explica con tarjetas bilingües y fuentes de la NASA. El juego funciona sin internet, en una red local.

Es importante porque los niños no solo ven el resultado de una misión: viven las decisiones que la hacen fracasar o tener éxito.
details:
What it does and how it works

Space Survivor is a two-player educational game in which kids ages 7–12 keep a Mars outpost alive. A level for middle school is also included.

  • Player 1 (student) uses a handheld controller we built. Its screen shows a pocket map of the base, like the second screen of a dual-screen console. The joystick moves the astronaut, the red, white and blue buttons choose shield, energy or water, the knob sets how much to give (0–100 %), and the green button confirms. The main game runs in the browser, which shows the animated base, resource levels and mission cards.
  • Player 2 (teacher) acts as Mission Control on Earth. From a separate computer, the teacher picks anomalies based on real solar events from NASA’s Space Weather Database (DONKI): flares, coronal mass ejections and particle storms. The teacher also decides when each one reaches the base and how many supply crates appear beforehand.
  • Warnings travel to Mars with a delay, like real radio signals. The student must collect supplies and split limited resources between zones before the event hits.
  • After each event, a bilingual card (Alert, Mission, Why?) explains what happened, what NASA would do and where the data comes from.

Benefits

  • It turns abstract mission trade-offs into decisions kids make with their hands: giving more to one zone always means less for another.
  • It gives teachers a ready-to-use lesson on space weather, radiation and life support, with the teacher in an active role.
  • It never says “game over.” The astronaut gets tired or weak and recovers, and the end screen gives a tip and a summary with badges, so failure becomes learning.
  • It works in any browser, with no installs or accounts, and runs on a local network without internet.

Expected impact

  • Classrooms, science clubs and families can use it to learn how real mission planners decide under limited resources and delayed communication.
  • Because it is bilingual (Spanish/English) and uses low-cost hardware, it can reach schools with limited budgets or poor connectivity.
  • Our next steps are testing it with students in real classrooms, adding pulse-sensor challenges and connecting live DONKI events.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Game and web views: JavaScript with Vite, HTML/CSS, Node.js server with WebSockets over a local network.
  • Game engine: pure, deterministic JavaScript with seeded randomness. 243 automated tests (Vitest and end-to-end) and a 1,000-mission simulator to balance the game.
  • Hardware: ESP32 (ESP-IDF), ILI9341 320×240 TFT screen, analog joystick, potentiometer, four push buttons and a 3D-printed case.
  • Data: NASA Open APIs and DONKI (FLR, CME, SEP, GST events from the last three years). NASA Science resources for the card facts and the Earth–Mars message delay.
  • Art: original illustrations generated with Python scripts, plus NASA images (Perseverance, Curiosity, Viking, Apollo 17, SDO) used with credits.

Creativity

  • Two roles instead of one: the teacher controls the “space weather” and the student lives with the consequences, which mirrors the real relationship between Mission Control and astronauts.
  • A physical controller with a map screen, so the resource split becomes something kids feel by turning a knob.
  • Communication delay as a game mechanic, which teaches why astronauts must act on their own.
  • “Paper NASA” art style: real NASA photos cut out like paper and combined with colorful paper illustrations.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: real events labeled “real NASA event” and invented ones labeled “game event.” Sources are shown inside the game, and archived data is never presented as live.
  • Age-appropriate design: few core resources, plain language, icons plus color for each state (so it does not rely on color alone), readable contrast and positive feedback.
  • No free choice: we simulated 1,000 missions to make sure no strategy is completely safe.
  • Accessibility and cost: any browser, offline local network, bilingual, affordable components.
  • Privacy: no accounts and no personal data stored.
